title: The Advocate
subtitle: How to change a system that was not built for you: independence, rights in writing, the escalation ladder, evidence, rulemaking, and building power with care partners
outcomes: Tell independent advocacy from industry-funded messaging, and check any group's funding yourself
Use the federal Conditions for Coverage to protect a patient, including against improper involuntary discharge
Escalate a problem in the right order, with documentation that holds up
Build an evidence case using public data and basic quality-improvement methods
Influence a federal rule or policy through comments, casework, and coalitions

scenes.text: Welcome to the last course. You've seen the machine and the gates. Now we turn to you. An advocate is not someone who is angry, and not someone who is nice. An advocate is someone who changes outcomes, for one person or for many, with facts, persistence, and independence.

Start with independence, because the kidney world is crowded with voices that sound like patients but are paid for by the industry. That is not a conspiracy theory. It is in their own documents. One prominent patient organization says on its own funding page that it began in 2004 as DaVita Patient Citizens, with initial funding from a corporate sponsor, and changed its name in 2009 as funding expanded to multiple corporate donors.

v.title: One patient organization's history, in its own words

items.t: Founded as 'DaVita Patient Citizens', funded by a corporate sponsor
Renamed 'Dialysis Patient Citizens' as corporate donors expand
Lists corporate sponsors on its website

v.src: Dialysis Patient Citizens funding fact sheet

scenes.text: And you saw the American Kidney Fund in Course 1, with reported donations from the two largest dialysis companies around eighty percent of its 2018 budget. Organizations funded this way can do real good for individual patients. But when a policy fight pits patients against their funders, notice which way they lean.

v.text: Funding does not make a group wrong. It tells you which fights it is unlikely to pick.

scenes.text: You can check any organization yourself, in about ten minutes. Nonprofits file a public tax form, the Form 990, which shows revenue, executive pay and major programs. Lobbying is disclosed in the Senate and House lobbying databases. Payments from drug and device makers to physicians are public in the federal Open Payments database. Learn these three, and you will never have to take anyone's word for who they speak for.

v.title: Three public tools to check any voice
items: IRS Form 990: revenue, pay, programs (search ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer)
Lobbying Disclosure Act filings: who lobbies, for whom, on what
CMS Open Payments: industry payments to physicians and teaching hospitals

scenes.text: Let me show you how to read a nonprofit's tax form in five minutes, because it will change how you hear every press release. Search the organization on ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer. Open the most recent Form 990. Page one, Part One, shows total revenue and expenses. Part Seven lists what the top officers and highest-paid employees earn. Schedule I shows grants the organization gave away. The names of most individual donors are not public, but the organization's own website or annual report often lists corporate sponsors. Put those pieces together and you know who it answers to.

v.title: A Form 990 in five minutes
steps: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer
Part I: revenue and expenses
Part VII: officer and staff pay
Schedule I: grants given
Annual report: corporate sponsors
v.note: Who funds a voice tells you which fights it will avoid.

scenes.text: Open Payments works the same way for doctors. Go to the federal Open Payments search, type in your nephrologist's or surgeon's name, and you will see payments and transfers of value reported by drug and device makers: meals, travel, consulting fees, research money. A payment is not proof of wrongdoing. Many excellent physicians consult. But if your doctor is recommending a specific product, it is fair, and calm, to ask whether they have a relationship with the company that makes it.

v.text: A reported payment is not proof of wrongdoing. It is a reason to ask a calm, direct question about a recommendation.

scenes.text: Independence also matters inside your own care. Every dialysis facility has a medical director, usually a nephrologist, who is paid by the facility for that role. Physicians can also hold ownership stakes in clinics or access centers through joint ventures, which is lawful when structured within the rules, and which you saw at the center of the enforcement cases in Course 1. None of that makes a recommendation wrong. It does make it fair to ask, politely: do you have a financial relationship with this facility or this company? A good doctor will answer plainly.

v.text: "Do you have a financial relationship with this facility or company?" It is a fair question, and a good doctor answers it plainly.

scenes.prompt: Five questions to ask any group that claims to speak for patients. Tap each.

cards.b: Who funds you, and what share comes from companies that profit from kidney care?
Have you ever publicly opposed a position of your largest funder?
How many of your board members are patients or care partners with no industry ties?
What specific policy are you pushing right now, and who benefits if it passes?
Where can I read your Form 990 and lobbying filings?

scenes.text: The Cold Ischemia Foundation's answer to all five is public: it takes no funding from drug, biologic, device or pharmaceutical companies, or from dialysis organizations. That is the standard you should hold every voice to, including ours.

v.text: The patients and care partners who write to us are the only constituency we answer to.

scenes.text: One more thing defines a true advocate: you work on the system and the person at the same time. Fixing one patient's discharge is advocacy. Documenting the pattern so it stops happening to the next person is advocacy that compounds. Every module in this course gives you a tool for both.

items: Stop this discharge
Get this referral sent
Fix this bill
Document the pattern
Report it to regulators
Change the rule

scenes.text: Every dialysis facility that takes Medicare must follow a federal regulation called the Conditions for Coverage, found in Title forty-two of the Code of Federal Regulations, part four ninety-four. It is the single most important document most patients have never read. It turns 'please' into 'you must'.

v.sub: 42 CFR Part 494: the rules every Medicare dialysis facility must follow

scenes.text: Part of it is a section on patient rights. Among them: to be informed about all treatment options and settings, including transplantation and home dialysis; to be informed about and participate in all aspects of your care; to be told of your right to file grievances, inside the facility or outside it, without reprisal; and to be informed of the facility's policies for transfer and discharge.

v.title: Patient rights (42 CFR 494.70), selected
items: Be informed of all treatment modalities and settings, including transplantation and home dialysis
Be informed about, and participate in, all aspects of your care
File internal or external grievances without reprisal
Be informed of the facility's transfer and discharge policies
Receive the services in your plan of care

scenes.text: Two more rights you can use tomorrow. First, the rights must be visible. The regulation requires every dialysis facility to prominently display a copy of the patient's rights, including the mailing addresses and complaint telephone numbers of the state survey agency and the ESRD Network, where patients can easily see and read them. If you cannot find it, ask where it is. Second, your records. Under federal privacy law, you have the right to a copy of your medical records, and the provider generally must respond within thirty days, with one possible thirty-day extension.

v.title: Rights you can use tomorrow
items: Patient rights posted where patients can read them
Posting includes state agency and ESRD Network phone numbers
Right to a copy of your medical records (HIPAA)
Response within 30 days, one 30-day extension possible
v.src: 42 CFR 494.70(d); HHS: Individuals' right to access health information

scenes.text: The rights section reaches further than most people realize. It includes the right to be informed about advance directives and the facility's policy on them, and the right to be informed about the facility's own policies on patient care. It protects respect, dignity, privacy, and the confidentiality of your records. And it says you may file a grievance personally, anonymously, or through a representative. When something feels wrong at a clinic, start by asking a simple question: which of my written rights does this touch? Very often, the answer is more than one.

v.title: More rights in 42 CFR 494.70
items: Respect, dignity and recognition of individuality and personal needs: (a)(1)
Privacy and confidentiality in treatment and records: (a)(3), (a)(4)
Advance directives and the facility's policy: (a)(6)
Facility policies on patient care: (a)(8)
File grievances personally, anonymously or through a representative: (a)(17)

scenes.text: Now the most important protection of all: involuntary discharge. Being thrown out of a dialysis clinic can be deadly. So federal rules allow it only in four situations. The patient or payer stops paying. The facility closes. The facility can no longer meet the patient's documented medical needs. Or the patient's behavior is disruptive and abusive to the point that it seriously impairs the delivery of care.

v.title: The only four permitted reasons for involuntary discharge (42 CFR 494.180(f))
items: Nonpayment
Facility closure
Facility can no longer meet the patient's documented medical needs
Disruptive and abusive behavior that seriously impairs care delivery

scenes.text: And for that last reason, behavior, the facility has to follow steps. Document reassessments and its efforts to resolve the problem. Give the patient and the regional ESRD Network thirty days' notice. Get a written order signed by both the medical director and the patient's own physician. Try to place the patient at another facility and document it. And notify the state survey agency.

v.title: Required steps before a behavior-based discharge
steps: Document reassessments and efforts to resolve
30-day notice to patient and ESRD Network
Order signed by medical director AND attending physician
Attempt placement elsewhere, documented
Notify state survey agency
v.note: A shortened process is allowed only for immediate, severe threats to the health and safety of others.

scenes.prompt: A clinic tells a patient he'll be discharged next week for 'noncompliance' because he often leaves treatment early. Is that one of the permitted reasons?

options.t: Yes, noncompliance is a standard reason
options.fb: Noncompliance is not one of the four permitted reasons. Shortening treatment is a clinical problem to address, not grounds for discharge on its own.

options.t: No. Unless his behavior is disruptive and abusive enough to seriously impair care, and the required steps are followed, it isn't a permitted reason
options.fb: Right. Ask for the reason and the documentation in writing, and contact the ESRD Network and state survey agency immediately. A week is also less than the required 30-day notice.

options.t: It depends on what the clinic manager decides
options.fb: The rule is federal. A manager cannot add reasons that aren't in it.

scenes.text: Notice two things in that scenario. 'Noncompliance' is not on the list. And a week is not thirty days. Facilities don't always get this right, and patients almost never know the rule. Now you do. Write the citation down: forty-two CFR four ninety-four point one eighty, paragraph f.

v.text: Keep it handy: 42 CFR 494.180(f). Four permitted reasons. Thirty days' notice. Two physician signatures. A placement attempt. State notification.

scenes.text: Since May 2026, the official guidance surveyors use to inspect dialysis facilities lives in Appendix H of the State Operations Manual. If you ever file a complaint, citing the regulation and the survey guidance tells inspectors you know exactly what the facility was supposed to do.

items: Dialysis survey guidance moved to State Operations Manual, Appendix H
Includes new guidance for home dialysis in nursing homes
Telehealth flexibilities for home dialysis reflected

scenes.text: When you put a problem in writing, use a structure the reader cannot ignore. One: what happened, with dates and names. Two: the rule it conflicts with, by citation, if you know it. Three: the harm, or the risk of harm. Four: the specific fix you are asking for. Five: a reasonable deadline for a written answer. Keep it to one page. Keep a copy. Send it in a way you can prove, such as email or the facility's grievance form with a dated receipt. Calm, specific, documented. That is the voice that gets results.

v.title: A one-page grievance
items: 1. What happened: dates, names, facts
2. The rule it conflicts with, by citation
3. The harm, or the risk of harm
4. The specific fix you want
5. A deadline for a written answer

quiz.q: According to its own funding page, what was Dialysis Patient Citizens originally called?
quiz.why: It began in 2004 as DaVita Patient Citizens with a corporate sponsor and was renamed in 2009.

quiz.q: Which public document shows a nonprofit's revenue and executive pay?
quiz.why: IRS Form 990, searchable through tools like ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer.

quiz.q: Which database shows industry payments to physicians?
quiz.why: Open Payments discloses payments from drug and device makers.

quiz.q: Which of these is a permitted reason for involuntary discharge under 42 CFR 494.180(f)?
quiz.why: The four: nonpayment, closure, inability to meet documented medical needs, and seriously disruptive and abusive behavior.

quiz.q: How much notice is required before a behavior-based involuntary discharge (outside immediate severe threats)?
quiz.why: 30 days' notice to the patient and the ESRD Network.

quiz.q: Whose signatures must the discharge order carry?
o: Both the medical director and the patient's attending physician
quiz.why: Both physicians must sign.

quiz.q: What does the patient rights section say about filing grievances?
o: Patients may file internal or external grievances without reprisal
quiz.why: 42 CFR 494.70(a)(16): the right to file internal or external grievances, or both, without reprisal.

quiz.q: Under 42 CFR 494.70(d), what must a dialysis facility display?
o: Patient rights, with state agency and ESRD Network complaint numbers
quiz.why: Rights must be prominently posted, including complaint contact information.

quiz.q: Under HIPAA, how long does a provider generally have to respond to a request for your records?
quiz.why: HHS: generally 30 days, with one 30-day extension in some cases.

quiz.q: Which part of the Form 990 lists pay for top officers and highest-paid employees?
quiz.why: Part VII reports compensation of officers, directors and key employees.

sources.t: Dialysis Patient Citizens: Funding fact sheet
Undark: Kidney Dialysis Is a Booming Business (2020)
Code of Federal Regulations: 42 CFR Part 494 (govinfo, 2024 edition)
HHS: Individuals' right to access health information

scenes.text: When something goes wrong, the instinct is to go big right away: the news, a lawyer, social media. Sometimes that's right. Usually it isn't the first step. Problems get solved fastest when you climb a ladder in order, and each rung is documented, so that if you have to climb higher, you arrive with a record.

v.sub: Climb in order. Document every rung.

scenes.prompt: Put the escalation ladder in order, from first step to last resort.
items: Write it down: dates, names, what was said
Raise it with the care team, then file the facility's grievance
Contact the regional ESRD Network
File a complaint with the state survey agency
Contact your U.S. Representative's or Senator's caseworker
Public record: media, public comment, testimony
scenes.fb: Some problems skip rungs. An immediate safety threat goes straight to the state survey agency, and an emergency to 911. But for most problems, this order gets results and builds a record.

scenes.text: Rung one is documentation, and it is the rung people skip. Write down the date, the time, who was there, what was said, and what was promised. Ask for decisions in writing. If someone refuses to write it down, write down that they refused. Your notes, made at the time, carry weight later.

v.title: Documentation that holds up
items: Date, time, place, people present
Exact words where you can
What was promised, by whom, by when
Copies of letters, emails, notices
A note of any refusal to put things in writing

scenes.text: Rung two is the facility's own grievance process, which every Medicare dialysis facility must have and must explain to you. Rung three is the ESRD Network, a regional organization under contract with Medicare that handles patient grievances and monitors involuntary discharges. Rung four is the state survey agency, the inspectors who can cite a facility for violating the Conditions for Coverage.

v.title: Who can act on a dialysis complaint
items: Facility grievance process
ESRD Network (Medicare contractor)
State survey agency (inspections, citations)
HHS Office of Inspector General (fraud)
Congressional caseworker
Long-term care ombudsman (nursing homes)

scenes.text: A few practical details about the ESRD Network, because people hesitate when they do not know what to expect. You can call or write. You can ask that your name not be shared with the facility, though anonymity can limit what the Network can investigate. Ask for a case or reference number and the name of the person handling it. The Network can work with the facility on a resolution and can refer serious problems to the state survey agency. Write down every call, just as you would at the clinic.

v.title: Calling the ESRD Network
steps: Call or write
Say whether your name may be shared
Get a case number and contact name
Network works with the facility
Serious issues: referral to the state agency

scenes.text: Rung five surprises people. Every member of Congress has caseworkers whose job is to help constituents with federal agencies, including Medicare. A short, factual letter from a congressional office to an agency tends to get a response. And if you suspect fraud, billing for services not provided, or kickbacks, the HHS Office of Inspector General runs a hotline, and federal law protects whistleblowers who report it.

v.text: Congressional caseworkers exist to help constituents with federal agencies. They are free, and agencies answer them.

scenes.text: And fear of retaliation is real. Patients depend on the facility several times a week. That's exactly why the regulation protects the right to file grievances without reprisal, and why your documentation matters. If anything changes in how you're treated after you complain, write it down the same day. Retaliation itself is something you can report.

v.title: If you fear retaliation
steps: File in writing; keep a copy
Note how you are treated afterward
Report any change the same day
Escalate to the Network and state agency

scenes.prompt: A care partner has filed a facility grievance about repeated missed medications. Two weeks pass with no answer. What's next?

options.t: Post the clinic's name on social media
options.fb: That may feel good, but it skips rungs that have power to fix it, and can complicate the record.

options.t: Contact the ESRD Network with the dated grievance and notes, and ask about the state survey agency's complaint line
options.fb: Right. The Network can intervene, and the state survey agency can inspect and cite. The dated grievance proves you tried the facility first.
An unanswered grievance is evidence. Use it on the next rung.

scenes.text: Stories open doors. Evidence keeps them open. The most effective advocates pair a person's story with numbers that show it isn't one person. In this part of the module you'll learn where the numbers live, and how to use them without getting tripped up.

v.sub: Public data, and the statistics traps to avoid

scenes.text: Here are the sources you've seen all through these courses, and you can use every one. Medicare's Care Compare rates dialysis facilities. The Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients publishes reports on every transplant program, including how often it accepts organ offers and how quickly its patients get transplanted. Medicare publishes performance data on every organ procurement organization. And the Justice Department and HHS Inspector General publish every settlement.

v.title: Where the evidence lives
items: Medicare Care Compare: dialysis facility ratings and measures
SRTR program reports: transplant rates, offer acceptance, waitlist outcomes
CMS OPO performance data
DOJ and HHS-OIG enforcement releases
MedPAC reports to Congress
USRDS annual data reports

scenes.text: One example of how to read these sources. A transplant program report from the Scientific Registry shows, among other things, how often the program accepts organ offers compared with what would be expected, and how quickly its listed patients actually receive transplants. Two programs with similar survival rates can differ enormously in how many of their patients ever get transplanted. For a patient choosing where to list, that second number may matter most.

items: How recipients do after surgery
How many listed patients ever get transplanted
How often offers are accepted

scenes.text: Now the traps. Trap one: counts versus rates. A huge company will always have more complaints than a small one. Compare per one hundred clinics, or per thousand patients. Trap two: the denominator. A transplant program can look great by listing only the healthiest patients. Ask who was counted. Trap three: risk adjustment. Programs that take harder cases should be compared after adjusting for that.

v.title: Three statistics traps
items: Counts vs. rates: compare per 100 clinics or per 1,000 patients
The denominator: who was counted, and who was left out?
Risk adjustment: compare like with like

scenes.prompt: Clinic A had 40 complaints this year; Clinic B had 10. Clinic A treats 800 patients; Clinic B treats 100. Which has the higher complaint RATE?

options.fb: That's the count. Per patient, A is 40 ÷ 800 = 5 per 100 patients.

options.t: Clinic B: 10 per 100 patients, versus 5 per 100 for Clinic A
options.fb: Right. B's rate is twice A's. Always divide by the right denominator before you compare.
Compute both: A is 5 per 100 patients; B is 10 per 100.

scenes.text: The Cold Ischemia Foundation uses Lean Six Sigma, a quality-improvement discipline, to structure its analyses, and you can use its simplest tools. Define the problem in one sentence. Measure it with a rate. Map the process step by step, like the flowcharts in these courses. Find the root cause by asking why, five times. Then propose a fix, and a way to check that it held.

v.title: A simple improvement cycle (DMAIC)
steps: Define the problem in one sentence
Measure it as a rate
Analyze: map the process, ask why five times
Improve: one specific fix
Control: how will we know it held?

scenes.text: Let me show you the five whys with a real-world pattern. Patients at a clinic keep missing their transplant evaluation appointments. Why? They have no ride. Why? The medical transportation benefit only covers dialysis trips. Why does that matter? The evaluation is at a hospital ninety minutes away, on a different day. Why is nobody solving it? No one is assigned to schedule rides for evaluations. And why not? Because referral is tracked, but completion of the evaluation is not. Now you have a fix to propose: assign an owner and track completion, not just referral.

v.title: Five whys: missed evaluations
steps: Patients miss evaluations
Why? No ride
Why? Benefit covers dialysis trips only
Why unsolved? No one owns scheduling
Root cause: completion is not tracked
v.note: Fix: assign an owner and track completion, not just referral.

scenes.text: A Pareto chart is the other tool worth knowing. List every complaint you've collected, group them by type, and sort from most to least. Usually a few causes produce most of the harm. Bring decision-makers the top two, with numbers, and one fix for each. That is far harder to dismiss than a list of thirty grievances.

v.title: Example Pareto: complaints logged by a patient group (illustrative)
v.src: Illustrative example for teaching, not real data

scenes.text: Last rule of evidence: say exactly what your source says, and no more. If it's an allegation, call it one. If a figure is from 2017, say 2017. If it's a company's own number, say so. Your credibility is your most valuable asset, and one overstated claim can cost you a room you spent a year getting into.

v.text: Say what the source says, with its date, and no more. Precision is power.

scenes.text: Most of the rules you've learned about were written by federal agencies, not Congress. And federal agencies are legally required to ask the public before they finalize most rules. That is the most underused power patients have.

v.sub: How rules are made, and how to be heard in the room

scenes.text: Here's how it works. An agency like Medicare publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register. A comment period opens, often sixty days for major Medicare rules. Anyone can submit a comment on regulations dot gov. The agency must consider the significant comments, and respond to them, when it publishes the final rule.

v.title: How a federal rule is made
steps: Proposed rule in the Federal Register
Public comment period (often 60 days)
Agency reviews and responds to significant comments
Final rule published
Rule takes effect

scenes.text: For dialysis, this happens every single year. Medicare proposes changes to the dialysis payment system, usually in the summer, and finalizes them in the fall. Transplant rules like the organ procurement rules and the IOTA model went through the same process. So did the national transplant network's policies, which have their own public comment cycles.

items.t: Proposed ESRD payment rule: comment period opens
Final ESRD payment rule, with responses to comments
OPTN policy proposals open for public comment
Bills in Congress; letters to your Representative and Senators

scenes.text: What makes a comment count? Not volume. Agencies don't tally votes. A comment that changes a rule does four things. It names the specific section. It brings evidence: data, or a documented experience. It explains the real-world consequence. And it asks for one specific change, in plain words.

v.title: A comment that changes a rule
items: Names the specific section or proposal
Brings evidence: data or documented experience
Explains the real-world consequence
Asks for one specific, concrete change

scenes.text: The national transplant network has its own public comment process, separate from Medicare's. It opens comment periods, usually twice a year, on proposed changes to allocation, notification, living donation and more. Patients and families can read the proposals and comment directly on the network's website, and the committees read them. The 2025 proposal to notify patients about active and inactive status changes is one example: patient comments are part of its record.

items.t: Medicare and other agency rules, via regulations.gov
Transplant network policies, usually two comment cycles a year
Specific section, evidence, consequence, one clear ask

scenes.prompt: Which sentence would make the strongest opening for a comment on a transplant rule?

options.t: This rule is terrible and you should be ashamed.
options.fb: Anger is understandable, but it gives the agency nothing to act on.

options.t: Regarding the proposed patient notification requirement: I request you also require notice of organ offers declined on a patient's behalf, because patients cannot advocate for themselves without it.
options.fb: Right. Specific section, specific change, specific reason. That's exactly the gap you saw in Course 2.

options.t: Please make transplants better for everyone.
options.fb: Too general to act on. Name the provision and the change.

scenes.text: Congress is the other lever. The Restore Protections for Dialysis Patients Act, introduced after the Supreme Court's Marietta decision, is one example of legislation you can track and support or oppose. Your representatives' offices count constituent contacts on bills. A short phone call naming the bill and your position is logged.

v.text: Name the bill, state your position, give one sentence about why it matters to you. That's a contact that gets counted.

scenes.text: And use the calendar. Agencies and legislators respond to moments: a new report, a proposed rule, an anniversary, a hearing. The Cold Ischemia Foundation publishes something every week, with the Watch List on Mondays and the Gatekeeper Files on Thursdays. Those are ready-made openings to send your representative something concrete.

v.title: Moments that create openings
items: A proposed rule's comment period
A new MedPAC, USRDS or SRTR report
A Watch List or Gatekeeper Files release
A congressional hearing or bill introduction
An enforcement action in your state

scenes.text: When you write to an elected official, write for a busy staff member who will spend ninety seconds on it. Subject line: your town, the issue, and your ask. First sentence: who you are and that you are a constituent. Second: the problem, with one number and one human detail. Third: the specific action you want, such as cosponsoring a named bill, sending a letter to an agency, or asking a question at a hearing. Then one paragraph of evidence, your contact information, and thanks. Short letters get read. Specific asks get answered.

v.title: The ninety-second letter
items: Subject: town, issue, ask
Who you are: a constituent
The problem: one number, one human detail
The ask: one specific action
Evidence paragraph, contact, thank you

quiz.q: What is the first rung of the escalation ladder?
o: Document: dates, names, what was said and promised
quiz.why: Documentation makes every later rung stronger.

quiz.q: What is an ESRD Network?
o: A regional Medicare contractor that handles patient grievances and monitors discharges
quiz.why: Networks are Medicare contractors with a formal grievance role.

quiz.q: Who can inspect and cite a dialysis facility for violating federal rules?
quiz.why: State survey agencies inspect on behalf of Medicare.

quiz.q: Who should receive suspected billing fraud reports?
o: The HHS Office of Inspector General hotline
quiz.why: OIG investigates fraud; whistleblowers have legal protections.

quiz.q: Clinic A: 40 complaints, 800 patients. Clinic B: 10 complaints, 100 patients. Which has the higher rate?
Which source reports transplant program performance, including organ offer acceptance?
quiz.why: The Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients publishes program-specific reports.

quiz.q: What does a Pareto analysis show?
o: That a few causes usually produce most of the harm
quiz.why: Sorting problems by frequency points you to the few that matter most.

quiz.q: What is the 'D' in DMAIC?
quiz.why: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control.

quiz.q: Where are proposed federal rules published?
quiz.why: Proposed and final rules appear in the Federal Register; comments go through regulations.gov.

quiz.q: Do agencies decide rules by counting comments like votes?
o: No, they must consider and respond to significant comments on their substance
quiz.why: Substance matters more than volume.

modules.title: One Case and the Power of Care Partners

scenes.text: Let's put everything together with one case, start to finish. Meet Marcus. He's fifty-eight, on in-center hemodialysis for two years. His wife, Dana, is his care partner. Nothing about Marcus is unusual. That's the point. Everything that happens to him happens to people every week.

v.h: One Case and the Power of Care Partners
v.sub: Applying every tool in this course to one family

scenes.text: Week one. Marcus has been leaving treatment twenty minutes early because of severe cramping. A staff member tells Dana that if it keeps happening, Marcus will be discharged for noncompliance. Nobody has adjusted his treatment for the cramping. Dana is frightened, and so is Marcus. Missing treatment is dangerous; losing his clinic could be fatal.

v.text: Week 1: a verbal threat of discharge for 'noncompliance', and a medical problem no one has addressed.

options.t: Argue with the staff member at the front desk
options.fb: Understandable, but it leaves no record and puts Marcus in a harder position.

options.t: Write down what was said, by whom and when; then ask the nephrologist in writing to address the cramping, and ask for the facility's discharge policy
options.fb: Right. Documentation first, then a written request that turns the 'noncompliance' into the clinical problem it is.
Moving may be an option later, but leaving under threat surrenders his rights and his record.

scenes.text: Week two. Dana's note and request worked partly. The nephrologist adjusts the treatment, and the cramping eases. But Dana also asked a question nobody had asked in two years: has Marcus been referred for a transplant? The social worker checks. He hasn't. And there is no note explaining why, even though federal rules require the facility to evaluate every patient's suitability for referral and to document the reason when it decides not to refer.

v.text: Week 2: no transplant referral in two years, and no documented reason. That missing note is a violation of 42 CFR 494.80(a)(10) that Dana can cite.

scenes.prompt: Put Dana's next steps on the transplant referral in the right order.
items: Ask the social worker in writing why no referral was sent
Request that a referral be sent, with the date it will happen
Call a transplant center directly to ask about self-referral
Confirm the center received the referral and ask for the evaluation date
Note the date in the care map and follow up weekly
scenes.fb: Two tracks at once: push the facility to send the referral, and open the door from the transplant side. Because Marcus is on dialysis, his waiting time can be credited back to his dialysis start once he's listed.

scenes.text: Week six. The evaluation is scheduled. Then a letter arrives. Marcus will be involuntarily discharged in ten days. The letter cites disruptive behavior. Dana is stunned. The only incident on record is that Marcus raised his voice once, months ago, when his session was cut short.

items: Reason given: disruptive behavior
Notice given: 10 days
No documented reassessments or efforts to resolve
Signed by the facility administrator only

scenes.prompt: Tap each card: what's wrong with the letter under 42 CFR 494.180(f)?

cards.b: Ten days. The rule requires 30 days' notice to the patient and the ESRD Network for behavior-based discharges, absent an immediate severe threat.
Only an administrator signed. The rule requires a written order signed by both the medical director and the attending physician.
No reassessments or efforts to resolve. The rule requires them in the medical record.
One raised voice months ago. The rule requires behavior disruptive and abusive to the extent it seriously impairs the delivery of care.

scenes.text: Dana climbs the ladder, in order, the same day. She sends the facility a written grievance citing the discharge regulation, and the missing referral documentation. She calls the ESRD Network, which must receive notice of any involuntary discharge, and sends them the letter. She files a complaint with the state survey agency. And she calls their congressman's office and asks for a caseworker, because the discharge could cost Marcus both his treatment and his transplant evaluation.

v.title: Dana's escalation, same day
steps: Written grievance citing 42 CFR 494.180(f)
ESRD Network notified, with the letter
State survey agency complaint
Congressional caseworker

scenes.text: Within a week, the facility withdraws the discharge. Marcus keeps his chair and his evaluation date. Dana doesn't stop there. She sends the Network a short summary of what happened, asks whether other discharges at that facility have been reviewed, and joins a patient group that is preparing comments on next year's dialysis payment rule. One family's crisis becomes part of the public record.

items: Treatment adjusted
Referral sent
Discharge withdrawn
Pattern reported to the Network
Facility discharges reviewed
Joins public comment on the payment rule

scenes.text: Dana's notebook deserves its own lesson, because it won the case. Use one notebook, paper or digital, for everything. Each entry gets the date and time, who was there, what was said, what was promised and by when. Clip every letter and printout in date order behind it. Keep a one-line index at the front of every serious issue and its status. When you need to escalate, you will not be remembering. You will be reading from a record, and everyone in the room will know the difference.

v.title: The care notebook
items: One notebook for everything
Each entry: date, time, who, what was said, what was promised
Letters and printouts in date order
Front page: index of open issues and status

scenes.text: Notice what won. Not volume, not anger. Dana won with a notebook, three written requests, one regulation, and the order of the ladder. You now have every one of those tools.

v.title: What actually won
items: A dated notebook
Written requests that created a record
One regulation, cited precisely
The ladder, climbed in order, the same day
Follow-through that turned one case into evidence

scenes.text: When should you go to the press? Usually after you have climbed the ladder and documented the response, because a reporter's first question will be, what did they say when you complained? Get the patient's clear permission for anything about their health. Privacy laws bind providers, not patients, so a patient can share their own story, but they should decide exactly what to share. Keep to what you can prove, label allegations, and bring the documents. A story backed by records lasts. A story built on anger fades by the weekend.

items: Dated documentation
Written responses, or the lack of them
Patient consent to share
No written complaint filed
Facts you cannot prove
Someone else's private details

scenes.text: The last part of this course is about the people this system leans on the most and listens to the least. Care partners. The spouse who drives to treatment three times a week. The daughter who manages forty medications. The friend who learns to run a home dialysis machine.

v.sub: The unpaid workforce, and how to turn individuals into a force

scenes.text: In 2025, AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving estimated that sixty-three million Americans are family caregivers, a forty-five percent increase over a decade earlier. In kidney care, the system quietly assumes they will be there. Transplant programs often require a named support person. Home dialysis often requires a trained partner. Transportation to treatment falls on them.

v.label: Americans providing family caregiving, 2025
v.src: AARP and National Alliance for Caregiving, Caregiving in the US 2025

scenes.text: Yet care partners rarely have a formal voice. They can be left out of care planning, told they are not the patient, and burned out with no backup. If you are a care partner: ask the patient to name you in writing as someone the care team may speak with, and ask to be included in care planning meetings. The patient's right to participate in their plan of care includes choosing who helps them do it.

v.title: Protecting the care partner's role
items: Patient names the care partner in writing (privacy authorization)
Request inclusion in care planning meetings
Ask about respite and backup coverage
Check eligibility for job protections such as FMLA
Keep your own notes and copies

scenes.text: Care partners need protection too, and there is some. The federal Family and Medical Leave Act lets eligible employees take up to twelve weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave a year to care for a spouse, child or parent with a serious health condition. It can be taken in blocks, or intermittently, such as a few hours for appointments. Not every worker qualifies; it depends on the size of the employer and how long you have worked there. Ask your employer's human resources office in writing, and some states add paid leave on top of it.

items.label: month period the weeks are counted in

v.src: U.S. Department of Labor: Family and Medical Leave Act

scenes.text: And every care partner needs a backup. The system quietly builds itself around one dependable person, and when that person gets sick, burns out, or simply has to work, the whole plan wobbles. Name a second person. Put them on the care map. Ask the patient to authorize the care team to speak with them too. Share the binder. It is not a sign of weakness. It is the same thing a hospital does for every critical role: it never relies on one person alone.

v.text: The system leans on one dependable person. Name a second. A plan with one point of failure is not a plan.

scenes.text: Now, building power. One person with a documented complaint can fix one problem. Twenty people with the same documented complaint can change a facility. A few hundred, organized, can change a regulation. The difference is coordination: a shared record, a shared ask, and the patience to keep showing up.

scenes.prompt: Put the steps of a small advocacy campaign in order.
items: Pick one problem you can document
Collect stories and numbers from others affected
Find the decision-maker who can fix it
Make one specific ask, in writing
Follow up on a schedule, and publish the result
scenes.fb: Notice the first step: one problem. Campaigns fail most often by trying to fix everything at once.

scenes.text: You've already seen campaigns like this work. The race-based waiting time correction. The organ procurement accountability rules. Each began with people who documented harm, refused to accept the first no, and kept pressing for years. None began with power. They built it.

v.title: Change that started with documented harm

items.t: OPO outcome measures with real consequences
Waitlist status notifications; OPO accountability rule

scenes.text: Your story is your most powerful piece of evidence, so tell it with a shape. Sixty seconds is enough. Start with a moment, one specific scene. Then the problem behind the moment, in one sentence. Then one number that shows it is not only you. Then the change you want, and who can make it. Practice it out loud until it fits in a minute. You will use it with a reporter, a legislator, a hospital board, and a family in a waiting room who needs to hear that someone else made it through.

v.title: A sixty-second story
steps: One specific moment
The problem behind it
One number: it is not just you
The change, and who can make it

scenes.text: When you finish this module and its knowledge check, you will have completed every lesson in this course. Take the final assessment when you are ready. Score seventy percent or better and you will earn a certificate with your own number. But the certificate is not the point. The point is the next phone call you make, the next letter you send, the next family you help find their footing. That is how this foundation measures success: not in what we know, but in what you do with it.

v.text: The certificate is not the point. The next call, the next letter, the next family you help: that is the point.

scenes.text: So here is what I'll leave you with. You now know how the machine is paid, who owns it, where its gates are, which rules bind it, how to climb the ladder, how to use evidence, and how rules are made. Most people dealing with kidney disease will never learn any of this. You have. Use it for the person in front of you, and for everyone after them.

v.h: Now you know how the machine works
v.sub: Use it for the person in front of you, and for everyone after them

quiz.q: In Marcus's case, what was Dana's most important first action?
o: Documenting what was said and asking in writing for the cramping to be treated
quiz.why: Documentation plus a written clinical request reframed 'noncompliance' as a medical problem.

quiz.q: Which defect in the discharge letter violates 42 CFR 494.180(f)?
o: Only 10 days' notice and only an administrator's signature
quiz.why: The rule requires 30 days' notice and an order signed by both the medical director and attending physician, plus documented efforts.

quiz.q: Why did Dana also contact a transplant center directly?
o: To open the referral from the transplant side while pressing the facility to send it
To get a second dialysis chair
quiz.why: Working both sides of a stalled hand-off is faster than waiting on one.

quiz.q: About how many Americans were family caregivers in 2025, per AARP and NAC?
quiz.why: 63 million, a 45% increase over a decade earlier.

quiz.q: What's the most common reason small campaigns fail, as taught here?
o: Trying to fix everything at once instead of one documented problem
quiz.why: Pick one problem, one decision-maker, one specific ask.

quiz.q: What should a care partner ask the patient to do so the care team will speak with them?
o: Name them in writing as someone the team may speak with
quiz.why: A written authorization lets the care team share information with the care partner.

quiz.q: How much job-protected leave can an eligible employee take under the FMLA to care for a spouse, child or parent?
o: Up to 12 weeks unpaid per year
quiz.why: U.S. Department of Labor: up to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in a 12-month period.

quiz.q: What is the first element of a strong sixty-second story?
quiz.why: Start with a moment, then the problem, one number, and the change you want.

quiz.q: When is it usually right to go to the press?
o: After climbing the ladder, with documentation and the patient's consent
quiz.why: A reporter will ask what happened when you complained. Bring records and consent.

quiz.q: Why should every care partner name a backup?
o: So the plan doesn't fail when one person can't be there
quiz.why: A plan with one point of failure is not a plan.

final.q: What does independence mean for a patient advocate, as taught in this course?
o: Not being funded by, or answerable to, companies that profit from the care being judged
final.why: Funding shapes which fights a group will pick.

final.q: Which is NOT one of the four permitted reasons for involuntary discharge?
o: Facility can no longer meet documented medical needs
final.why: Noncompliance alone is not a permitted reason under 42 CFR 494.180(f).

final.q: What notice is required before a behavior-based discharge (absent an immediate severe threat)?
o: 30 days to the patient and ESRD Network
final.why: Plus two physician signatures, a placement attempt, and state notification.

final.q: Which rung usually comes before contacting the state survey agency?
final.why: Climbing in order builds the record; immediate safety threats are the exception.

final.q: Which public database shows industry payments to physicians?
Clinic X: 30 complaints, 300 patients. Clinic Y: 30 complaints, 1,500 patients. Which has the higher rate?
What makes a public comment most persuasive?
o: Specific section, evidence, consequence, and one concrete ask
